description: Mobile Village at DEF CON 25 covers mobile security and wireless exploitation with 4 talks on LTE impersonation, GPS spoofing, NFC vulnerabilities, and Android reverse engineering.

talks.title: Ghost Telephonist Impersonates You Through LTE CSF
talks.teaser: LTE cellular network impersonation attacks enabling identity spoofing and call interception.
talks.summary:
### Architectural Flaws in LTE Circuit Switched Fallback
At 00:00, Yuwue Zheng and Lin Huang introduce their discovery of a critical vulnerability in the 4G LTE Circuit Switched Fallback (CSFB) mechanism. In telecommunications networks that have not fully transitioned to Voice over LTE (VoLTE), 4G smartphones must temporarily fall back to legacy 2G or 3G networks to complete incoming and outgoing voice calls or SMS delivery. The researchers discovered that during this transitional handover procedure, the 3GPP protocol specification omits essential authentication validation steps.

### Exploiting the Authentication Void in CSFB
At 07:15 and 14:20, the speakers walk through the signalling flow between the User Equipment (UE), the LTE base station (eNodeB), the Mobility Management Entity (MME), and the 2G/3G Mobile Switching Center (MSC). When a network triggers CSFB via a paging request, the handset switches to the legacy cell without mutual authentication. An adversary operating a rogue Software-Defined Radio base station (using OpenAirInterface) can intercept this transition and hijack the subscriber's signalling session.

### The "Ghost Telephonist" Attack Scenarios
At 20:25, the presenters demonstrate the alarming real-world ramifications of the "Ghost Telephonist" attack. By intercepting the unauthenticated CSFB handover, the attacker can impersonate the victim's phone number to place unauthorized outgoing calls, redirect incoming calls to eavesdropping endpoints, or intercept SMS two-factor authentication (2FA) verification codes. Crucially, this attack does not require cracking the subscriber's SIM card encryption keys or gaining physical possession of the device.

### Telecommunications Carrier Realities and Bypass Demos
At 28:50 and 34:10, Zheng and Huang analyze how the vulnerability impacts major cellular operators internationally. They conduct live laboratory demonstrations showing an attacker successfully intercepting banking password reset tokens sent via SMS and hijacking incoming voice verification calls. The researchers discuss how network-level optimizations implemented by carriers to reduce call setup latency inadvertently widened the timing window for rogue base station injection.

### Remediation Strategies and VoLTE Acceleration
Concluding around 40:43, the authors discuss technical mitigations for mobile network operators and standards bodies. They emphasize that the definitive long-term solution is accelerating the full deployment of Voice over LTE (VoLTE), which keeps voice and data unified on authenticated 4G packet networks. For legacy 2G/3G infrastructure, they recommend enforcing mandatory paging response authentication in MSC controllers to block rogue handover hijacking.

talks.title: Man in the NFC
talks.teaser: NFC interception and relay attacks on mobile payment and communication systems.
talks.summary:
### Near Field Communication Architecture and Practical Use Cases
At 00:00, Haoqi Shan and Jian Yuan open by surveying the widespread global adoption of Near Field Communication (NFC) technology. Operating at 13.56 MHz, NFC powers essential daily interactions, including contactless credit card payments (EMV), smartphone payment systems (Apple Pay, Android Pay), electronic transit ticketing, and physical building access control badges. Because NFC is designed for ultra-short communication ranges (typically under 4 centimeters), developers often mistakenly presume that physical proximity guarantees security.

### Classification of Contactless Card Protocols
At 06:12 and 11:30, the speakers review the international standards governing contactless cards, focusing on ISO/IEC 14443 Type A, Type B, and Sony FeliCa. They explain that while underlying radio frequencies remain standardized across all categories, different application standards implement drastically divergent security architectures—ranging from unauthenticated plaintext memory reads in legacy transit cards to cryptographically secured dynamic tokenization in modern EMV banking applets.

### Constructing the "Man in the NFC" Hardware Proxy
At 16:50, the authors reveal their custom hardware interception platform: the "Man in the NFC" proxy. Built using affordable microcontrollers, FPGA signal slicers, and active RF transceivers, the device operates as an active relay emulator. One module emulates a contactless smart card to trick legitimate POS payment terminals, while the companion module emulates an NFC reader to interrogate genuine victim cards, bridging transactions over extended physical distances via high-speed wireless or Bluetooth links.

### Exploiting Transit Protocols and Offline Transaction Limits
At 24:10 and 28:45, Shan and Yuan showcase practical attack scenarios against transit systems and offline payment profiles. They demonstrate modifying data packets on the fly between reader and card, altering transaction value registers or spoofing terminal capabilities. Because many automated turnstiles and vending machines utilize offline transaction caching to maintain rapid commuter throughput, forged cryptograms and modified responses succeed without triggering instant bank rejection.

### Countermeasures and Hardware Verification
Concluding around 33:35, the presenters outline defensive engineering recommendations for NFC hardware designers and software developers. They advocate enforcing strict transaction response timeout windows (distance bounding protocols) to prevent wireless relaying, utilizing mutual cryptographic authentication for all memory block queries, and securing point-of-sale firmware against malformed APDU buffer overflow attacks.
